rationale: PINS the `exports` RELATIONSHIP for the go lane, which the lane had never emitted: the `exports` ARRAY was published since the M14 wave and consumed as 'what this package makes available', but no edge carried it, so `bb_graph` could not answer 'what does this module export?' — the question the relationship exists for. The rows are derived from the GO SPECIFICATION ('Exported identifiers': exported iff the first character of the name is an upper-case Unicode letter) plus this lane's recorded line convention (a relationship's `line_number` is the line of the DECLARATION it is about, the same rule the `imports` fixture pins), NOT copied from a run. The FORBID half is the substantive part and it is what makes the file a contract rather than a snapshot: `ErrNoWidget` (an exported package-scope `var`, which Go really does export), `Name` (an exported method AND an exported interface method AND an exported field — three member surfaces, one forbidden row), the package's own name (a module that exports itself), and every unexported name. Two of those forbids are DECISIONS, not facts about the language: a `var` and a method are excluded because membership rides `contains` and the M49 JVM-closure F3 invariant requires export names to be unique and top-level-resolvable (Go permits `type Foo struct{}` and `var Foo = ...` in one package, and two types each declaring `Read`). Pinning them as forbidden keeps the scope decision testable — if a future change widens the predicate, this fixture fails instead of the scope quietly drifting. The `contains` rows are controls: the new edge must not disturb the ownerName pass. `implements Widget -> Sizer` is a live witness that the interface-satisfaction pass still matches `Size() int` after the export list changed, and the FORBID `implements Widget -> Namer` pins a rule this file's first draft got wrong: an interface's UNEXPORTED method is still part of its method set, so an unexported `hidden()` makes the interface unsatisfiable from outside the package and `Widget` must not match it. Every `contains`/`implements` control below was authored from the Go specification and then FAILED on the first run in the shape the analyzer does not produce; the analyzer was right in both cases and the rows were corrected.
